items.body:
STROOM fills in a gap on the timeline, excavating vital experiments made in Cologne in the wake of the cult 'Novaya Scena' compilation by Svitlana Nianio, Michael Springer, Guido Erfen, Soloveyka, Yewgeny Taran and Wolfram Burgtorf.

Back in 1993, a bizarre 20-track compilation appeared from Cologne's musical fringe. The idea for the set had come from artist and producer Erfen and sound engineer and percussionist Springer, two close friends who, taking advantage of cheap rent and disused buildings, put on regular events and established a recording studio in their neighborhood, off the beaten track. Erfen was a dedicated tape trader and had received a transmission from Kharkiv's Novaya Scena rock club that arrived with an essay and music from three local bands. At this time, Ukraine was still under Soviet rule and the music fascinated the two friends, shining a spotlight on a part of the world they were completely unfamiliar with. When singer and keyboardist Soloveyka visited cologne a year later, she handed Erfan more tantalizing music, inspiring him to make his own pilgrimage to Ukraine to investigate further. The research resulted in the 'Novaya Scene' CD, a set of tracks recorded between 1986 and 1992 that muddled prog with new wave, punk, folk and avant-garde rock. It was released on Hamburg's What's So Funny About label and was supposed to have a sequel.

That's where 'Aftermath and Transitions' comes in. Following the release of 'Novaya Scena', Erfen and Springer set up a series of sessions at their studio, inviting some of the Ukrainian artists to record with them. It's this period that resulted in Svitlana Nianio's 'Transilvania Smile' soundtrack that was properly released for the first time on Muscat sublabel Shukai in 2023. Nianio had been a member of Cukor Bila Smerť (the band who'd provided the stylistic anchor for 'Novaya Scena') and took the opportunity to launch her solo career, with Springer working as engineer. And there was more material from those sessions that Springer held back: the compilation's first four tracks are collaborations between Nianio, Springer, Taran and Springer's good friend Burgtorf. Opener 'Fake' was almost finished when Nianio showed up at the studio with her Casio in tow, so Springer plugged her in and she ended up lavishing the beat with vocals in Ukrainian and oddball keyboard vamps. The other three tracks were a little more organic, improvised in the studio while the artists got familiar with one another - there's the decelerated reggae experiment 'ManySpace', the instrumental groover 'Quiet Place' and best of all 'Політ Світляки', a wiry percussive jam that's not aged a day.

Erfen joins in on the ace exotica-tinged 'Whispering Walls' and 'Tired River', tracks from the group's final session in 1995. Nianio and Taran were planning to renew their visas and return to Cologne to record more, but it never happened - the recordings were shelved and the artists went about their lives independently. Then there's the three Solar tracks recorded by Soloveyka and Burgtorf who struck up a friendship after meeting at Springer's studio. Singing in Russian and English, Soloveyka breathes cabaret energy over Burgtorf's jerky, sample-heavy ethno-groove productions. And it's left to Taran to finish things off, with a "1996 Version" of his 'Death and the Bachelor' track that features none other than Nianio on keys. Phew. It's a brilliant set, really - not just one for STROOM obsessives, it'll speak to anyone whose interest in the Ukrainian underground was piqued by 'Transilvania Smile' or Muscut's ace Cukor Bila Smerť anthology.

items.body:
Constructed in a vacuum from naked FM synth sounds and discreet concrète elements, 'Clock In, Clock Out' is a set of atemporal experiments that exist in their own ecosystem - essential listening if you're into Motion Graphics or Visible Cloaks' enduringly influential 'Fairlights, Mallets and Bamboo' mix.

Xavier García Bardón and Emmanuel Gonay's second release following 2021's brief Lexi Discs 7" 'Aταραξία / Καταστροφή', 'Clock In, Clock Out' sounds reactionary in its own way, completely eschewing current production norms to lock into an airless atmosphere that's at odds with established logic. It makes the record captivating to listen to; there's no real density, very little (if any) reverb, almost no digital processing. As far as we can tell, it's just percussive synth sounds, silence, acoustic drums and a handful of other sounds that seem to fit Bardón and Gonay's methodology. The context appears to be revealed on 'Endnotes', the record's final track, when slow renaissance-era lute strings are plucked to shadow the synthesised sounds we've already heard on the previous tracks. A bell chimes and city sounds leak into the duo's hermetically sealed chamber and it feels unsettling. Going back to the beginning and listening all over again, the unsettlingly artificial sounds begin to make even more sense.

Bardón and Gonay don't make modern early music or nostalgic synth gear, they make sounds that exist on their own timeline. The metronome that they reference in the title is marking years as much as it's marking tempo. Are we listening to the early '80s when we hear FM sounds that Paddy Kingsland and Peter Howell might well have used when they were holed up in the BBC Radiophonic Workshop's windowless studio? Or beamed to the decade's close when the duo recycle the E-mu Emulator II 'Loon Garden' sample that 808 State famously used on 'Pacific State'. It's more complicated than that; the phrases themselves sound older, more ancestral and they're interrupted by seemingly human outbursts that Musica Mosaica sample and distort. Each track seems to exist in the same unsettling uncanny valley, 'Tempistica Metronomica' welding together a web of percussive sounds into glassy a-rhythmic glissando slides and 'Concaténations' sounding like an orchestra virtual bottles being blown by clockwork automatons. 

It's over far too quickly, but it's one of the weirdest, most perfectly self-contained sets we've heard in ages. Huge recommendation.

items.body:
Booting off the new year with his most urgent set in years, Shackleton follows his flawless run of psychedelic future-ancient excursions with a lissom body of left-foot-fwd bangers chiseled specifically for the soundsystem.

If you've only tuned into Sam Shackleton's latter-day material - those s-tier collaborations with Heather Leigh, Marlene Ribeiro, Holy Tongue and Six Organs of Admittance, or even his jaw-dropping 2023 solo tome 'The Scandal of Time' - you can be forgiven for ignoring his earlier, sticker gear, the foundational bass variations that proposed a parallel course for dubstep and his destructive work with scene architects like Pinch, Appleblim and T++. On 'Euphoria Bound', he applies the skills and philosophies he's refined over the last few years traversing the outer perimeters of prog, psych folk and Carnatic music to the dancefloor, re-examining and rethinking his approach without sacrificing any of the thrust. These aren't winding, side-long lattices of rhythm and prismatic, xenharmonic animation, they're taut, shockingly direct bass variations that transmit the same uncompromising message.

There's not a dull moment here, but the best early example might be 'Crushing Realities', a concertinad six-minute marvel that seems to distill so much of Shackleton's most vital elements. He almost sounds as if he's remixing his own body of work, carving into dusty, microtonally skewed vocal snippets and zither chimes with rounded, woody syncopations that split the difference between Midori Takada and Peverelist. But it's not a single element that gives this one its signature; Shackleton's blotter-assisted fractal pattern of tape stop effects, vanishing voices, rhythmelodic sequences and battered radio static is only strengthened by the neck snapping flurry of kicks and undulating basslines. It's classic Shackleton in so many ways, reaching back to canonical faves like 'Blood on My Hands' and his remix of Moderat's 'Rusty Nails', and yet it sounds as if the producer is furtively ushering us towards uncharted territory.

The direction is marked out even more visibly on 'The Unbeliever's Pulse' when Shackleton interrupts hard swung, hollow thuds with synthetic sweeps and swooshes - analog pulses and haunted drones that sound as if they've been snatched from Conrad Schnitzler's archives. There's a trace of vintage UKG in there somewhere (think Wookie or Groove Chronicles), but Shackleton upsets the rhythm with decaying dub echoes. Where Shackleton's earliest uptempo experiments were guided by the rapid momentum of bass music and his omnivorous interest in spiritual jazz, industrial music (particularly Muslimgauze) and global psychedelia, 'Euphoria Bound' folds in on itself, assessing a catalogue that now covers the length and breadth of his passions. There are few producers who manage to keep up their levels for quite so long, and even fewer who can refresh their palate so flawlessly.

items.body:
Posthumous reminder of MF Doom’s landmark classic, following the late, great MC’s death at the end of 2020 - with 11 tracks of bonus material.

A staple of our listening diet upon release in 2004 (probably preceded or followed by a listen to his ‘Special Blends volumes), ‘MM….Food’ still stands up among the greatest and most coveted hip hop albums of our time. Beats to bars, it’s a peerless example of Daniel Dumile Thompson’s MF Doom alias, playing out as a sort of stoned comic book fantasy voiced by a cartoon supervillain, literally inspired by Marvel Comics’ Doctor Doom, whose moniker sounds a bit like MF’s real middle name.  

The album oscillate between Doom’s mind-boggling metaphoric wordplay and his signature instrumentals, adapting the golden era ‘90s style of sampledelic collage and rugged rhymes to his singular purpose, and making a marked step on from his earlier work as Zev Love X with the legendary KMD. By choice or osmosis there’s probably a whole generation of headz who’ve committed the bars of ‘MM….Food’ to memory, and we can only recommend a refresher session right here if you’re rusty. Packing bags of nostalgia and vibes for days, it’s a true evergreen.

items.body:
Deepchord producer Rod Modell’s fruitful binds with Silentes’ 13 series yields its lushest outing yet, following in the glistening wake of Gigi Masin & Taka Noda jams to this elemental bliss out.

‘Grotto Of The Sun’ limns a metaphorical and physical thawing of Modell’s sound, in suit with the natural processes described on his ‘Frequencies in the Fog’ and ‘Northern Michigan Snowstorms’ albums. Exquisitely textured recordings of running water and birdsong are recombined with synthetic sound sources and diffused into a pair of durational tapestries that settle dead easy on the mind.

The presence of syrupy subbass lets you know we’re still in Modell’s hands, umbilically tied to dub techno, but it’s all much closer to the intentions of Japanese environmental ambient and adjacent new age in its esoteric outlook and contemplative outlook.

Crackshot rap x club hybridiser Andrea Corradi splices dozens female spitters and mutant beats on ‘Outtakes’, the 2nd of his tapes for Reel Torque - Big RIYL DJ Screw, Rabit, Bobby Beethoven, Croww, Clams Casino, Hud Mo, Shadetek...

After his first volume sold out in a minute, Italian sound artist Andrea Corradi returns with a heat-seeking follow-up, shelling a 90 minute carousel of exclusive edits on tape, replete with a bonus 31 digital components for the DJs on an included download. It’s a rowdy cut ’n splice ram-raid that imagines; what would X rapper sound like on Y beat? The abundant results explore myriad permutations of this rudely unbalanced equation, from aggro jit paired with double speed fire, to Cerwin Vega-testing subs squashed with bitchiest bars, and genuine WTF‽ juxtapositions that go incredibly hard. 

The title ‘Outtakes’ knowingly undersells the prime material inside, which hits wider and just as rude as the ‘Ichinoya’ motherload which reached Mary Anne Hobbs’ BBC Radio 6 show and rinsed The White Hotel earlier this year. All the material lives up to expectations, firing from-the-hip mercurial fusions of underground, female rappers with leading-edge club ructions, with particular focus on mapping mutual, metric sweetspots between tunes that were never supposed to go together, but clearly work a treat. 

It’s effectively one of the canniest exercises in locating the mythical “3rd track” that we’ve heard in a hot minute, nailing the transitory pleasure of on-the-fly blends with a game sense of daring and rude empathy that rewards many happy returns in its spectrum of surprises - especially if you’ve had a keen ear on these pages over the years.

items.body:
At this point you shouldn’t need any introduction to Liz Harris.. She’s got a few albums and splits under her belt now, but chances are the first time you came across her music was the stunning modern classic ‘Dragging A Dead Deer Up A Hill’, released back in 2008.

It was the distinct and singular blend of shimmering dreampop and tape-mangled noise that had just about anyone worth their salt in awe of her music, so you can imagine the hype surrounding this one. Ah, but then it’s not only one record is it? A I A is two full forty minute full-lengths, and rather than a traditional double, these are two distinct albums, each one with its own focus and style. ‘Alien Observer’ might be the more outwardly song-based of the two, and while the songs aren’t necessarily as clearly defined as those on ‘Dragging A Dead Deer Up A Hill’, they slowly and pointedly push up through Liz’s familiar, hazed layers . Her distinct tones are barely audible over the mudded harmonies, starting life as ghostly echoes, but the further you get into it, more clearly defined shapes start to emerge.

It's music that no doubt changes with each listen – you're left to fill in the gaps - and while we can hear the heaving breaths of the Cocteau Twins, The Red House Painters and This Mortal Coil wrenching themselves from somewhere, we'd probably come to a different conclusion on the next listen. ‘Alien Observer’ is a markedly different record from its predecessor, and comes across as a deeply thoughtful blend of the harrowing, sincere experiments of Liz’s early records and the sort of songwriting that lodged ‘Heavy Water’ in our collective memory back in 2008.

items.body:
Totally mesmerising ’70s Ghanaian highlife, licked with palmwine guitar and subtly in step with US soul as much as traditions rootsy sound, which made it a domestic bestseller at the time.

"A defining recording of the era, Sikyi Highlife bridges tradition and innovation at a pivotal moment in Ghanaian music. Deeply rooted in the classic 1950s–’60s highlife sound, K. Gyasi drew inspiration from the ancient sikyi drum-dance of the Akan people of southern Ghana, shaping the album’s rhythms around its distinctive pulse. The vocal arrangements echo the traditional Akan modal style, grounding the music firmly in Ghana’s cultural heritage. Yet Sikyi Highlife is equally forward-thinking. As electric guitars became standard in highlife during the 1960s, the 1970s ushered in further experimentation. The Noble Kings broke new ground as the first highlife guitar band to incorporate keyboards and a full horn section into their sound, expanding the genre’s sonic possibilities while retaining its rootsy spirit.

Gyasi’s approach was part of a broader indigenisation movement among Ghana’s electric highlife bands in the post-independence era. Inspired by the nation’s ‘African Personality’ ethos and reinforced by Afrocentric messages arriving from American soul and funk, artists began reclaiming traditional forms within modern arrangements. Contemporaries included Koo Nimo, who revived the older palmwine style, and drummer Nii Ashitey, whose Wulomei band pioneered a folklorised Ga highlife sound from 1973.

Like many musicians of his generation, Gyasi was a passionate supporter of Ghana’s independence movement. In 1963, he travelled as a musical ambassador alongside Ghana’s first president, Kwame Nkrumah, performing across North Africa and the USSR and carrying Ghanaian culture onto the world stage.

The Noble Kings’ mid-’70s line-up featured some of the country’s finest musicians, including guitarist Eric Agyeman (who led the band at the time), Thomas Frimpong on drums and vocals, Ernest Honny on organ, and bassist Ralph Karikari - who was renowned for his innovative technique of translating the rhythms and tonal language of the traditional talking drum onto electric bass.

Upon its original release, Sikyi Highlife became one of the biggest-selling albums of the 1970s for Essiebons, earning Gyasi the affectionate honorary title of “Dr” from his devoted fans. Today, the album remains an evergreen classic, still cherished across Ghana and beyond."

Originally released in 1976 on Piero Umiliani’s own Sound Work Shop imprint, Drammi e Speranze -issued under the pseudonym Rovi - stands as a refined example of his late-period library work.

"Performed by a compact string ensemble and subtly augmented by piano, Hammond organ, Eminent organ, and Rhodes, the album unfolds through a series of classically-informed compositions where melody takes center stage. Each piece is concise, evocative, and purpose-built - reflecting the functional yet highly expressive nature of Italian library music at its peak.

Conceptually, the record is structured in two contrasting halves: the first side explores themes of optimism and resolution, while the second delves into darker, more introspective territories, mirroring the emotional duality suggested by its title (Tragedies and Hopes). Long overlooked outside specialist circles, Drammi e Speranze is here presented for the first time ever on vinyl reissue, newly remastered to highlight the depth and tonal richness of Umiliani’s arrangements. This release celebrates 100 years since the birth of Piero Umiliani, honoring the enduring legacy of a composer whose work continues to resonate across cinematic, library, and contemporary sample-driven music."

Jim O'Rourke and Jos Smolders team up again with the follow up to their first collaboration, Additive Inverse from 2021.

"Over a period of three years, both artists worked in sessions of a day, each in their own studio. The result is sometimes like a warm cloud of sounds, suddenly breaking up into a rhythmic, irregular pattern, after which it dives into introverted mindsets. The music is in constant flux.

The project followed the same workflow, but this time Jim took the lead and kicked off with a salvo of sounds that he extracted from his Kyma System. Both Jos and Jim were quite interested in the spectral character of sounds. Jim applied Kyma algorithms while Jos granulated his basic recordings. That way, textures are built, quite slowly moving from warm to gritty, from hard surfaces to deep sonic wells."

First released by Drexciya’s James Stinson and Gerald Donald in 1999 after establishing a cult reputation via EPs and 12”s for UR, Rephlex and Warp, ’Neptune’s Lair’ was issued by Berlin’s Tresor to the acclaim of those in the know. Since James Stinson died in 2002, in subsequent years the album has become widely regarded as their definitive opus - a hugely sophisticated, imaginative piece of Afrofuturist sonic fiction embedded with deeply rooted politics.

As the album approaches its 23rd anniversary of release, it still holds the power to utterly transport us to other dimensions. Using the ocean and water as metaphor for deep space, and by extension a site of the unknown, where far-fetched (but not entirely unreasonable) ideas about slave babies thrown overboard on slave-trade routes evolved into futuristic, practically alien beings, Drexciya, much like Sun Ra and his Saturnian roots, formed a whole world unto themselves thru their music, track titles and Abdul Haqq’s artwork, creating a sort of holistic gesamtkunstwerk as rich in subtext and noumenal flights of fancy as the most cult comic books or underground animation and cinema. 

In context of the very late ‘90s, when ‘Neptune’s Lair’ was issued, these ideas were necessary and important, as the electronic paradigm had been largely whitewashed by labels, promoters and DJs who either didn’t understand, or didn’t want to understand, the roots of the worldwide dance phenomenon that cropped up a decade prior - one mostly generated by PoC based in urban US cities. It’s perhaps as important as ever to acknowledge Drexciya’s origins and intent, to historically hold their work up to the rest of the field as waves of new, plugged in dancers become enthralled by their Hi-Tech Sci-Fi.

Classic.

items.body:
High impact, sound designer-sculpted industrial techno drama by french engineer-artist Franck Vigroux, shifting away from Mika Vainio worship to a more personalised sound, comparable to Mondkopf, an amped up JMJ, or Thomas Bangaltar’s ‘Irreversible’ OST.

“French composer and sound artist Franck Vigroux returns to raster with a new album called »Sonnailles«, set for release this spring.Conceived as a sequence-driven work, »Sonnailles« unfolds through a series of tightly structured musical passages interspersed with fragments of voices that appear within the compositions like ghostly presences. These vocal shards drift through the sonic landscape, punctuating Vigroux’s dense electronic textures and amplifying the album’s sense of tension and movement.

At the heart of the project lies a deliberate contrast: the collision of raw, almost primitive sonic force with an underlying sense of compositional sophistication. Vigroux crafted the music with an ear for immediacy and physical impact, exploring how rough textures and driving rhythms can coexist with intricate sound design.The album was also inspired by two unusual invitations that pushed the artist beyond his typical performance environments: a rock and punk festival in France and a series of techno club performances in China. These contexts led Vigroux to imagine music whose primary purpose was to move bodies on the dance floor — an approach that marks a new direction in his work.

For Vigroux, the challenge was particularly compelling. Alongside his musical practice, he frequently collaborates with dancers and stages multidisciplinary performances known for their radical physicality. With this new album, he brings those parallel worlds together, completing a circle in his ongoing exploration of the relationship between sound and the moving body — where composition, rhythm, and physical motion converge.”

Belgian avant-pop outfit Sergeant return to STROOM with a second album and a new member. RIYL Milan W, Total Blue or Animal Collective.

Since 2023's self-titled debut album, movie bro Benjamin Cools and actor Ferre Marnef have invited a new artist into the fold. The project was initially conceived as a live band, so the additional personnel just allows Sergeant to spread their creative wings; 'Symbols' is a more complicated record than its predecessor, packed out with byzantine arrangement and layered compositions, but it's also tighter. There's a feeling that their influences - '80s DIY pop, krautrock and post-punk - have been more fluidly lashed together this time around and Marnef's voice sounds more assured bedded in his collaborators' woozy, sometimes spiky productions. 

If their last record was "DJ Shadow in reverse", made from collaged elements and half-songs, 'Symbols' is a suite of proper compositions that dissolve as they play out, with tempos fluctuating and components mutating and vaporizing as Marnef sings. It's pop music that's engineered with Martin Hannett's ear for wacked-out production - fans of Ariel Pink (before he went full fash) or Panda Bear's 'Person Pitch' should investigate without delay.

items.body:
Originally released in 1972, "Universe In Blue" has been remastered and expanded to include two extra tracks from the same era. Phenomenal music, it shows a distinctly low-key, stripped-down side to the Arkestra, with Sun Ra on organ throughout.

It doesn't take long to tune into the mood of "Universe In Blue"'s chilly title track. With Sun Ra on his "intergalactic space organ" accompanied by sparse, barely-audible drums, Kwame Hadi on trumpet and John Gilmore on horn, it's a longing blues improvisation that gets to the gooey core of Ra's appeal. This is the sound of Alabama's deep sadness, channelled through ancient and modern technologies that heave through the almost 15-minute composition as Ra leads with monastic charm, lashing the church to the juke joint. June Tyson brings a confident, blown-out vocal performance to 'When the Black Man Ruled This Land' (conspicuously truncated to 'Blackman' on the original issue), emoting over Ra's organ blasts. It's the album's most upfront cut, allowing cracks of sunlight to part the darkness for just a second.

'In a Blue Mood' meanwhile continues where the title track left off, centering Ra's emotional organ jamming over skeletal drums, allowing the texture and timbre of the electric organ the space to cough and splutter emotionally. Anyone who already knows the record will no doubt be interested to pick thru the two additions: 'Discipline 27-II' and 'Intergalactic Research'. Both have been released before but not collected with this exact material, and both were recorded in 1972, so while they hover around a different mood - this ain't sedate organ blues - they capture Ra in the same creative tidal wave.

Budapest-based concept label, Blue Sun launches their new line of vinyl focused releases, aimed primarily on DJs and collectors: the Blue Series. A counterpart to the Orange Series launched in 2025 that showcases a more upbeat side of the label, the new collection presents a darker, more experimental, and introspective musical vision.

"The first release in the Blue Series is a six-track EP by Budapest based multimedia artist, Virág Réti. Choosing her legal name as her artist persona (“Flower of the Meadow" in Hungarian) also with the track titles capturing the folk names of local fauna, Peremidő evokes the artist's innate connection to nature as a place of refuge from the noise of Eastern European urban life.

The EP’s motifs point back to early memories of sitting by a river, simply observing time flowing by. The arc of the songs follow the passage of a day, beginning with the hesitant sounds of early morning, gradually moving on toward more defined, rhythm-driven forms. As the airy textures slowly give way to structure and percussion comes to the forefront, the sense of direction becomes clearer, letting moments of gentle disorder and unexpected sounds to surface.

Virág previously appeared on the label’s Blue Sun VA II compilation with her track Bíbic. Since launching her ambient music project in the fall of 2024, she has become one of the promising newcomers in the Hungarian experimental electronic music scene. Her debut EP, Minden Ami Megmaradt (All That Remains), was released last November as the final offering of temporary nites label (2023–2025). She is also the founder and organizer of the Budapest-based experimental electronic event series Still Places."

items.body:
Chicago quartet U.S. Maple's best album, 'Acre Thrills' is an American avant-rock masterpiecce that torches established formula unremittingly, singlehandedly creating music that's never quite been repeated - or bettered. Essential listening FFO Gastr del Sol, Hella, even black midi.

By the time U.S. Maple released 'Acre Thrills' in 2001, they'd already proved what they needed to prove, building up a so-called "math rock" sound out of the bones of Captain Beefheart's deconstructed 'Trout Mask Replica' and tearing it apart on the fly. And even when they brushed with the college rock underground's top levels, opening for Pavement and potentially glomming onto a completely new audience, they stuck to their guns, getting weirder rather than sanding down their sharp edges. This album isn't as dark as its predecessor by any means (we're gonna blame 'Talker' producer Michael Gira for that one), but it's more delicately arranged somehow - a perfectly imperfect lattice of angular, xenharmonic riffs and interlock'd polyrhythms that still somehow manage to couch vocalist Al Johnson's almost inhuman groans and monologues. His delivery's like Marmite, undoubtedly, but it's another element of the U.S. Maple sound that makes them impossible to properly replicate - despite bands endlessly trying ever since.

Although 'Acre Thrills' almost relishes its own knottiness, it's packed with moments that sound almost welcoming, at least to us. Opener 'Ma Digital' is surprisingly soft, Johnson's voice just a low hum underneath Mark Shippy and Todd Rittman's pretty breezy, almost hummable riffs, and if you didn't know better, you might confuse 'Babe' for a bluesier post-hardcore experiment, like Karate through a blender. By 'Untitled' though, their claws are fully on show with an instrumental that deconstructs itself as it plays through, falling apart into run-out-groove noise that's supposed to make you question what you're listening to. And when the album jolts back to life with 'Obey Your Concert', it's bolder, trickier and edgier, with Johnson veering from David Thomas to David Bowie in a matter of seconds. In the wrong hands, this kind of studied, hyper-technical grandstanding would be like nails on a chalkboard, so it's genuinely shocking that U.S. Maple managed to make it sound not just effortless but enduringly edgy. It's not noodly prog, it's grinding, painful, urgent music that understands the all-important polarity of blues, rock and all its variants.

Italian ambient maestro Gigi Masin returns to his happy place on 'Movement', following 2020's 'Calypso' with a record that surveys a quarter century of vintage back room sounds, pulling from kosmische, new age, early techno, glitch and balearic house. 

For the last few years, Masin has been busy with a litany of collaborations, working with Jonny Nash and Young Marco as Gaussian Curve, with dub techno OG Rod Modell on 2023's 'Red Hair Girl at Lighthouse Beach and with jazz pianist Greg Foat on a ruck of soundtrack-y downtempo material. In fact it's been years since his last solo release; the Apollo-released 'Calypso' came out six years ago and 'Movement' appears to pick up where it left off. The waterlogged, sun-bleached concept is all but gone, but the sounds, cherry-picked from across the downtempo spectrum, are very much in keeping. 

Opener 'Bed on Mars' is classic Masin and should appeal to fans of his cult 1986 breakout 'Wind', the long-overlooked album that featured 'Clouds', that new age/ambient anthem that relaunched his career after it was sampled by both To Rococo Rot and Björk. It's a fleeting moment, but it's packed to the brim with the good stuff: humid post-Vangelis pads, synthetic choirs and reflecting pools of reverb. And the atmosphere's pierced by loping rhythms almost immediately; 'Lost' matches its elasticated brass moans with a low-slung beat and then 'The Age of Sampling' appears to hark back to the Fairlight era, conjuring up an industrial soundscape with jerky low-bitrate drum hits, dialog samples and inclement textures that sound like they belong on Black Rain's 'Neuromancer' soundtrack.

The title track is even more surprising, a slippery 120bpm house groover that sounds as if it's been precision engineered for hazy sunrises, with sax wails and vocal pads ducking behind its rubbery beats. If that sounds a bit much, then there's a few quieter spells, like the piano-led 'UMI' and the Shuttle358-inspired closer 'Fifteen', but you can tell that for Masin, "ambient" doesn't mean beatless. The highlight, 'Deception Dance', sounds like classic beardy back-room techno, even - the sort of twitchy biz Carl Craig used to engineer when he was still moonlighting as 69.

Thessa Torsing (aka upsammy) and drum deity Valentina Magaletti consolidate their intentions on 'Seismo', rustling up an illusory combo of artificial and live sonics - properly RIYL early Squarepusher, Matmos or Mira Calix.

When roles are so clearly demarcated, it can be hard to keep things challenging. Magaletti's a percussionist first and foremost, while Torsing is clearly happiest working on the DAW or behind the decks, but neither artist wanted their collaboration to be quite so predictable. So they figured out a way to make their respective roles  a little more complicated; after recording Magaletti's acoustic parts in Amsterdam's labyrinthine Rijksmuseum, Torsing decided to compliment them with digital percussion - mallet-style instruments that mimic or at least harmonize with Magaletti's elements. The result is a puzzling assembly of samples, sequences and breathless improvisations that injects some much-needed energy into the '90s Artificial Intelligence scaffolding Torsing has been respraying for the last few years.

Opener 'It comes to an end' yanks us back to Squarepusher's beardy jazz crossover era, or Matmos's ace early electroacoustic experiments. But Torsing and Magaletti keep things fresh, offsetting their ornate biomechanical flurries with Reich-ian minimalist phrases and xenharmonic prangs that keep us on our toes. It's unashamedly percussive material and yet plays like a sequence of lullabies, its virtuosic drumwork (just check the smoove editing on 'Superimposed') almost inevitably offset by music box chimes or cloudy, dreamlike pads. The other element that sets the duo apart is the vocals; peppered throughout the album are dialog snippets that keep things confusing, countering their surreal twangs and iceberg-cracking whirrs with alien whispers that only just permeate the membrane.

Is there even a voice on 'Hyperlocalize', or is it just our imagination? We can't be quite sure. But the garbled syllables are more audible on 'Mementoes', sandwiched between soothing, rubbery lead synths and hallucinated xylophones. Needless to say, if you're into anything from Plaid to Midori Takada, this'll be worth a closer listen.

Returning after a 13 year absence, Boards of Canada's vision of hell isn't exactly surprising, swapping out the magic hour guitars of 'The Campfire Headphase' and the tired Carpenter-isms of 'Tomorrow's Harvest' for jagged distortions, dialog snippets and uneasy religious symbolism.

It can't be easy for Mike Sandison and Marcus Eoin; as soon as they cracked the code with 'Music Has the Right to Children' in 1998, their home-brewed signature sound - tape-warped, reverb-soaked monosynths, stuttering dialog samples and thumping MPC-breaks - became a sort of meme, regurgitated by a wave of bedroom musicians so frequently that the original references became fully hollow. Those early records were great because they sounded so unique, marking a landscape littered with post-'Chiastic Slide' crunches and choppy AFX-ian amens with new channels of thought. Just go back to their shadowy 'Twoism', 'Hi Scores', or that Mask 500 cover of 'Midas Touch' -  there was nowt else like it. By the time we got to 'The Campfire Headphase', a comparatively sunny, guitar-led misstep that arrived a few years later and then 2013's 'Tomorrow's Harvest' -  it all felt like diminishing returns.

'Inferno''s mysterious VHS rollout also felt overly familiar - and if you're gonna tease, the payoff best be worth it. Sadly, first single 'Prophecy At 1420 MHz' was damp and old fashioned, lumpen with boxy '80s drums and awkward prog rock synths - the signs didn't look good. Heard as a whole though, 'Inferno' hangs together pretty well. The brothers do a good job of laying out a vision of hell that's intricately connected to their well-worn source material: the lost future that was promised to wide-eyed 1970s kids raised on color TV, welfare and action figures. Back then, religious cults and street cranks were screaming of damnation, convincing weakened minds that judgement was coming while the Vietnam War raged - real hell was on the doorstep all along. And it's hard not to hear Boards' blend of seemingly old-fashioned religious symbolism (the Hare Krishna chants, chopped-up divinity school lectures and guided meditations) as an indirect reference to the wars raging right now. Certainly, it's their darkest album in years; not the aesthetic darkness of 'Tomorrow's Harvest', either. 'Father and Son', with its eerie Abrahamic symbolism, feels like an American Gothic reflection of Leslie Nielsen's comparatively benign narrations on 'Geogaddi', while 'Memory Death' feels like Boards actively sending off their own patented brand of hauntology with the EKG blip to prove it.

Throughout the record, BoC appear to juxtapose a cultural concept of hell with their own aesthetic responses, balancing dystopian robot voices with squelchy acid gurgles on the excellent 'The Word Becomes Flesh' and Bobby Beausoleil-style chiming strings on 'Blood in the Labyrinth'.  'The Process', meanwhile, offers a late-stage vision of aviation hell, a 'Langoliers'-style horror cue that neatly precedes the saccharine vintage BoC hit of 'You Retreat in Time and Space'. Perhaps unsurprisingly, it's these beatless moments that really hold things together - maybe they should have just leaned into it and done a full length of those vignettes. Still, 'Inferno' has its moments.
